turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: Well I think it's worth saying at Stripe we are trying to do something I think relatively unique, which is what we power for the businesses to build on Stripe our users, it's really business critical to them. We're literally talking about money coming into your business to help you run your operations or make it even possible for you to run your operations and maybe pay your employees and so forth. All the revenue automation that we do around billing subscriptions, our financial automation products, helping you close your books, this stuff matters. You cannot get it wrong. And we also operate, Stripe today, we move as much money as all of e-commerce was when Stripe got started. So we operate very significant scale and so business critical significant scale, we just have a tremendous duty to our users to get this right and be extremely reliable and available for them. (00:53:23): So we do think about that a lot. Now there's one way to be very reliable, which is to try to change things as infrequently as possible. Never change anything than you have many fewer opportunities for things to break. But we don't take that approach. The needs of our users are evolving so rapidly, the number of ways that we want to serve them and can serve them is evolving rapidly enough that it matters a lot that we can operate in a kind of constantly changing environment. Hopefully I've explained why that matters like that type feedback because it's only possible if you can actually get something in their hands. So we choose to design the way we work to hold those two things true at the same time and it does take a lot of care and attention and it takes a lot of systems. So maybe just kind of build this up. (00:54:12): First of all, there's a lot in our development process and the ways that we take changes into our product that makes this possible. One of those is we really care a lot about having really good test suites. So we believe in automated testing. We don't have manual testers because manual testers couldn't possibly cover the vast array of API endpoint and configurations that we offer but automated test can. So we work hard to have a lot of automated test coverage and then every single change that an engineer produces gets run through this battery of tests before it can even possibly go towards production. And then we work very hard as changes end up in production to put them through increasingly realistic and then more broadly exposed environments. So we have a bunch of staging environments where we'll send a battery of more realistic end-to-end tests. Then finally when something actually goes to production, it starts at very small percentage of the traffic and then wraps up to the hole. (00:55:10): So we can detect problems before they become huge problems. There's a number of things that we had to do to make that all possible. So for instance, every change that Strip engineer submits [inaudible 00:55:23] test, it actually ends up in production automatically over the course of the next 45 minutes or so. And I don't think there are a lot of financial services companies, at least not until maybe the last few years that have operated that way. And so that takes a certain mind shift. You actually have to assume that that's going to happen and put the right systems and processes in place. And then the other thing that's important is to recognize that we have to obsess about getting very systematically good at addressing anything that can go wrong. So I mentioned earlier it's really important to me that we are a continuously learning organization. (00:55:59): And I mean something else that matters of course is things will go wrong. Sometimes there is a downstream partner where something breaks, other times there is a particular kind of network outage side of our control or whatever. So things will go wrong. So it's important that we have the right systems in place that minimize the damage that any individual thing going wrong can cause. And we work hard on that. We have redundant systems in a bunch of places. We think hard about how something that breaks for one user wouldn't kind of carry over into other users and then we actually very actively work hard to put things right when they are wrong. So that's called instant response at most companies including Stripe. I actually think Stripe is very, very good at instant response. We've got very good tools for both declaring incidents and then pulling the right people together to put them right. (00:56:45): But we don't stop there. We really obsess about reviewing them carefully and identifying not only what would've stopped this thing happening, but how could we prevent this whole class of issues in the future. And as I said earlier, we prioritize working on that stuff ahead of anything else on the roadmap that's because of remember what it is we're trying to do, how important it is and how if we don't do that well, we can't move quickly for our users. So that's how we do it. (00:57:09): By the way, I don't want to come across here and sound like we've got it all figured out. Of course all of this is always entirely influx. We're always anxious to figure out how we can make it go better. For instance, in recent years we realize that we could get a lot of benefit from what we call chaos testing. That's like injecting errors and making sure that the systems respond in such a way that it doesn't cause any impact on users. So it's constantly evolving and we really enjoy learning from other companies and learning from our users as well. But it's something we care about and think very rigorously and systematically alone.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为值得一提的是，在 Stripe，我们正在尝试做一些我认为相对独特的事情，这就是我们为企业在 Stripe 上构建我们的用户提供的动力，这对他们来说确实是至关重要的业务。我们实际上谈论的是进入您的企业的资金，以帮助您运营您的业务，甚至使您有可能运营您的业务，并可能支付您的员工工资等等。我们围绕计费订阅、我们的财务自动化产品所做的所有收入自动化，帮助您结账，这些都很重要。你不会弄错的。今天我们还运营 Stripe，我们转移的资金与 Stripe 刚开始时所有电子商务的资金一样多。因此，我们的运营规模非常大，业务关键型规模也非常大，我们对用户负有巨大的责任，确保做到这一点，并为他们提供极其可靠和可用的服务。 (00:53:23)：所以我们确实经常考虑这个问题。现在有一种非常可靠的方法，那就是尝试尽可能少地改变事情。永远不要改变任何东西，这样破坏东西的机会就会少得多。但我们不采取这种方法。用户的需求变化如此之快，我们想要为他们提供服务以及能够为他们提供服务的方式的数量也在快速变化，以至于我们能够在不断变化的环境中运营非常重要。希望我已经解释了为什么这种类型的反馈很重要，因为只有当你真正能得到他们手中的东西时才有可能。因此，我们选择设计工作方式来同时实现这两件事，这确实需要大量的关注和关注，并且需要大量的系统。所以也许只是建立这个。 (00:54:12)：首先，我们的开发过程以及我们对产品进行更改的方式使这一切成为可能。其中之一是我们非常关心拥有真正好的测试套件。所以我们相信自动化测试。我们没有手动测试人员，因为手动测试人员不可能涵盖我们提供的大量 API 端点和配置，但自动化测试可以。因此，我们努力进行大量的自动化测试覆盖，然后工程师产生的每一个更改都会经过一系列测试，然后才能投入生产。然后，我们非常努力地完成生产中的变更，让它们经历越来越现实、然后更广泛暴露的环境。因此，我们有很多临时环境，我们将在其中发送一系列更真实的端到端测试。最后，当某些东西真正投入生产时，它开始时只占流量的很小一部分，然后就结束了。 (00:55:10)：这样我们就可以在问题变成大问题之前发现它们。为了使这一切成为可能，我们必须做很多事情。例如，Strip 工程师提交的每项更改 [听不清 00:55:23] 测试，实际上都会在接下来的 45 分钟左右的时间内自动投入生产。我认为没有很多金融服务公司，至少在过去几年里不会以这种方式运营。因此，这需要一定的思维转变。实际上，您必须假设这种情况将会发生，并采取正确的系统和流程。另一件重要的事情是认识到我们必须致力于非常系统地解决任何可能出错的问题。所以我之前提到，我们是一个持续学习的组织对我来说非常重要。 (00:55:59)：我的意思是其他重要的事情当然是事情会出错。有时下游合作伙伴会出现问题，有时会出现我们控制范围内的特定类型的网络中断或其他情况。所以事情就会出错。因此，重要的是我们必须建立正确的系统，以最大限度地减少任何个别问题可能造成的损害。我们为此努力工作。我们在很多地方都有冗余系统。我们认真思考对某个用户造成的影响如何不会影响到其他用户，然后我们实际上非常积极地努力在错误时纠正错误。这在包括 Stripe 在内的大多数公司中被称为即时响应。事实上我认为 Stripe 非常非常擅长即时响应。我们拥有非常好的工具来报告事件，然后将合适的人员聚集在一起以纠正事件。 (00:56:45)：但我们并不止于此。我们非常着迷于仔细审查它们，不仅确定什么可以阻止这种事情的发生，而且确定我们如何才能防止将来出现此类问题。正如我之前所说，我们将这些工作优先于路线图上的其他任何事情，因为记住我们正在尝试做什么，它有多重要，以及如果我们做得不好，我们将无法为我们的用户快速采取行动。我们就是这样做的。 (00:57:09)：顺便说一句，我不想​​在这里听起来好像我们已经解决了所有问题。当然，所有这一切总是完全涌入的。我们总是渴望弄清楚如何才能让它变得更好。例如，近年来我们意识到我们可以从所谓的混沌测试中获得很多好处。这就像注入错误并确保系统的响应方式不会对用户造成任何影响。因此它在不断发展，我们非常喜欢向其他公司学习，也向我们的用户学习。但这是我们关心并单独进行非常严格和系统思考的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you say that it takes only 45 minutes from pushing code to it going into production?
turns.zh: 你是说从推送代码到投入生产只需要 45 分钟吗？

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: Typically yes. So that battery of tests that I described, that gets run on every change, that gets run in parallel to when you send it for review by another human. So it's run once, typically takes about 15 minutes and then once the changes merged into our code base, we run that same test suite one more time. So another 15 minutes then typically takes about 30 minutes for the systems to automatically deployed in production. That's how we run and think about establishing that tight feedback loop with users, that means you can get feedback from a user in the morning, you can figure out how to address it and you can actually put something back in their hands by the end of the day. And that loop running inside of 24 hours I think is pretty important.
turns.zh: 通常是的。因此，我描述的一系列测试会在每次更改时运行，并且与您将其发送给另一个人进行审核时并行运行。因此，它运行一次，通常需要大约 15 分钟，然后一旦更改合并到我们的代码库中，我们就会再次运行相同的测试套件。因此，再过 15 分钟，系统通常需要大约 30 分钟才能在生产中自动部署。这就是我们与用户建立紧密反馈循环的方式，这意味着你可以在早上从用户那里得到反馈，你可以找出如何解决它，并且你可以在一天结束时将一些东西放回他们手中。我认为 24​​ 小时内运行的循环非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. I remember times that Airbnb where took hours for tests to finish because there's a lot of them and they fix that over time. But I'm used to more on that scale.
turns.zh: 那真是难以置信。我记得 Airbnb 有时候需要几个小时才能完成测试，因为测试数量很多，而且他们会随着时间的推移修复这些问题。但我已经习惯了这种规模。

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: It takes constant effort to hold. Those numbers by the way are important. Those are about the right numbers I think for a company operating our kind of scale. Of course as you add more stuff, you add more tests. So we've had to work on, we had to invent mechanisms to make it run more in parallel, we now have a thing called selective test execution where we figure out for not the battery that runs before it goes into production that we run everything and just run it in more machines to make it parallelize. But for the changes or the tests that we run for individual changes, we actually have systems that figure out, well which tests are the ones that might be material for this particular thing? And that's been a real source of innovation. In fact, our distributed change and test environment at Stripe is the biggest distributed system that we actually run. And so running that requires just as much energy and effort and rigor and craft as everything else.
turns.zh: 需要不断的努力才能坚持下去。顺便说一句，这些数字很重要。我认为对于一家经营我们这种规模的公司来说，这些数字是正确的。当然，当您添加更多内容时，您就会添加更多测试。所以我们必须努力，我们必须发明机制来让它更多地并行运行，我们现在有一种叫做选择性测试执行的东西，我们发现在投入生产之前运行的电池不是我们运行的所有东西，而是在更多机器上运行它以使其并行化。但是对于我们为个别更改运行的更改或测试，我们实际上有系统可以弄清楚哪些测试可能对这个特定的事情是重要的？这是创新的真正源泉。事实上，我们在 Stripe 的分布式变更和测试环境是我们实际运行的最大的分布式系统。因此，跑步与其他事情一样需要精力、努力、严谨和技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some of the things you've done that have had the most impact on developer productivity?
turns.zh: 您所做的哪些事情对开发人员的生产力影响最大？

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: We've touched on a couple of these already. That auto deploy mechanism definitely had a very significant individual impact. So before we introduced that, sometime within the last five years each deployed to production required an engineer to actually babysit it, to watch it as it, make sure all the charts look good. And it was a bit of kind of game of roulette because you always wish that your change would get bundled in with someone else's so that they were paying attention to it for you. So literally being able to be fingers on keyboard on something else while your change is going live and it's going to automatically monitored, that was a big improvement in our productivity. Also, very small things. This is just like optimizing checkout, very small changes really compounded in a big way. So for instance, by eight months ago we made it possible, we use a tool for code review. (01:00:24): It's quite popular, it's GitHub enterprise, but we've built a bunch of our own experiences and controls around that and we have a little tick box that you can tick on your pool request. That's what you call an individual change that an engineer produces that is auto merge, which means once the reviewer says this is good, I don't need to come back and look at it again, the system should just take over and that just cuts out one whole kind of human distraction step and that laddered up to a big change in productivity as well. So these very small changes can if you're deliberate with them, ladder up to a big impact.
turns.zh: 我们已经谈到了其中的一些。这种自动部署机制无疑对个人产生了非常重大的影响。因此，在我们介绍这一点之前，在过去五年内的某个时候，每个部署到生产中的项目都需要一名工程师来实际照顾它，观察它，确保所有图表看起来都很好。这有点像轮盘赌游戏，因为你总是希望你的零钱能与其他人的零钱捆绑在一起，这样他们就会为你关注。因此，当您的更改生效并且将自动监控时，实际上能够将手指放在键盘上做其他事情，这对我们的生产力来说是一个巨大的提高。还有，非常小的事情。这就像优化结帐一样，非常小的变化实际上会产生很大的影响。例如，八个月前我们使之成为可能，我们使用了代码审查工具。 (01:00:24)：它非常受欢迎，它是 GitHub 企业版，但我们已经围绕它构建了一系列我们自己的经验和控制，并且我们有一个小复选框，您可以在池请求上勾选。这就是你所说的工程师产生的自动合并的单独更改，这意味着一旦审阅者说这是好的，我不需要再回来看它，系统应该接管，这只是消除了一种人类分心的步骤，这也导致了生产力的巨大变化。因此，如果你深思熟虑，这些非常小的改变可以产生巨大的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to go in a different direction now. AI very hot right now. Has AI impacted the way you all build product yet? And if not, where do you think it starts to go in the next few years?
turns.zh: 我现在要走向不同的方向。 AI现在非常火。人工智能是否影响了你们构建产品的方式？如果没有，您认为未来几年它会走向何方？

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: Yeah, we're very excited about AI. Now to just take one step back, Stripe has been using machine learning and advanced machine learning techniques at the heart of our products since the very early days. Radar is our solutions for payment fraud and it has used, I mean this is the very core of our products and has used machine learning since we introduced it. We also, if you think about the nature of Stripe, we operate in an environment where we have to do a lot of work to kind of catch bad actors in the system, fraudsters or fraudulent businesses. So we've been employing a lot of machine learning techniques there again for years and we couldn't operate the company without them. So the difference between ML and AI, I think when we think about AI today we're mostly talking about the applications of large language models, but those are really based on this new technology called Transformers. (01:01:55): It was a paper that came out of Google a while back about four years ago, five years ago. And we put transformer technology into those systems at some point more than a year ago. And it's proved to have a very profound impact on our ability to solve those problems for our users, which is great. But we are also excited about the applications of large language models. I mean there's really two dimensions to this. Number one, we feel privileged to be able to help serve and power a lot of businesses getting started in this space. One big difference between AI startups and others is it's actually quite expensive to operate an AI startup in terms of the compute resources. Like running this stuff in these GPU machines is quite expensive. So typically these companies need to have a monetization model from day one. And I'm really excited to say most of the AI on these is running on Stripe and we're working very hard to make sure we serve all their needs. (01:02:51): Open AI, for instance, using us for monetizing chat GPT plus and all their other products. But they don't just stop there. We're actually helping power all of their subscriptions and revenue tracking and financial operations around the business. And the point about that is we've been putting very large engineering teams on this stuff for years and that means anyone who wants to build a reconciliation product and a subscriptions business model, if you want to do that yourself, you have to put big engineering teams on them. But if you can use Stripe instead, you can actually focus those really precious engineering resources on keeping up with the rate of breakneck innovation in this space. So we're excited about that, but we're also really excited about the applications of these AI techniques on our own ability to serve our users better. And so for instance, at sessions we'll be talking about a few of these. (01:03:44): We started working with OpenAI when they had the beta. It was a kind of private beta of GPT four available at the beginning of this year. The first thing we thought of was we've got a lot of documentation on Stripe and we put a lot of care attention into making it good. But if you want to achieve something with your Stripe integration, you're typically going to spend quite a lot of time reading docs and kind of synthesizing them as an end user. We realized we can have GPT four read all of our docs, store them as embeddings and then answer questions for developers. And so we now have that available in kind of early stage release inside of our documentation. It's turning out to be pretty valuable. We've also been able to apply these techniques to other areas of our products. So something that we're going to show an early version of IT sessions is we have a really powerful product as part of our revenue and financial automation suite, which we call Sigma. (01:04:36): It allows you to write sequel queries across all of your Stripe data so you can interrogate your Stripe data to understand your business and really fine grain detail. Which country has the fastest growing sales, which segment in which country has particular attributes to it? Very powerful product, but it's one that is potentially challenging for non-developers to adopt. You do have to know how to write sequel queries unless you just use the ones in the menu in order to get the full value out of the product. Well it turns out with large language models, we can apply this technology where you can ask questions in natural language and our engine will actually write the sequel query for you. And we've had to do a lot of work to kind of tune that to make sure that it's reliable and understandable and it's going really well. And we also see great applications in actually applying these technologies to make us more efficient internally, answer users questions faster, help each other out more quickly. And so we're doing those things as well. One concrete thing that we did, which I'm pretty excited about is not long after we saw chat GPT come out, we realized it would be really awesome if we could apply that to many use cases inside of Stripe. But as you can imagine, a lot of the data that we are dealing with on a daily basis is very sensitive to our business, to our users and we care a lot and we have a lot of governance around this, but we wanted to make that technology bill. We couldn't say, Hey Stripes, go and use chat GPT. So we stood up an integration to GPT four and an internal UI to use models like that. But here's the thing that I want to kind of relate to all of your viewers. We find that we built presets into that. (01:06:12): So when you work with large language models, you want to write a prompt that then helps get the model into a state where it's going to be able to solve the particular problem at hand. And we find that writing prompts is something that's accessible to folks across lots of different job families, not just engineers. Folks in our marketing team, folks in our user support team have been able to use this as well. But you can put a lot of care and attention to getting a prompt that works really well and we not make it possible for those to be shared across the company. So I can grab the preset to help me write a blog post with the right kind of tone and I find it extremely valuable in helping me and many other people across the company. So I think there's a lot of innovation in high companies serve their users and operate is possible right now and we are working hard to employ all of that on behalf of our users.
turns.zh: 是的，我们对人工智能感到非常兴奋。现在退一步来说，Stripe 从一开始就一直在我们产品的核心中使用机器学习和先进的机器学习技术。雷达是我们针对支付欺诈的解决方案，它已经使用了，我的意思是这是我们产品的核心，并且自从我们推出它以来就使用了机器学习。另外，如果你考虑一下 Stripe 的本质，我们的运营环境必须做大量工作才能抓住系统中的不良行为者、欺诈者或欺诈企业。因此，我们多年来一直在那里使用大量机器学习技术，没有它们我们就无法运营公司。因此，ML 和 AI 之间的区别，我认为今天当我们考虑 AI 时，我们主要谈论大型语言模型的应用，但这些实际上是基于称为 Transformers 的新技术。 (01:01:55)：这是一篇大约四年前、五年前谷歌发表的论文。一年多前，我们将变压器技术引入这些系统。事实证明，它对我们为用户解决这些问题的能力产生了非常深远的影响，这非常棒。但我们也对大型语言模型的应用感到兴奋。我的意思是这实际上有两个维度。第一，我们很荣幸能够帮助服务和支持许多在这个领域起步的企业。人工智能初创公司与其他初创公司之间的一大区别是，就计算资源而言，运营一家人工智能初创公司实际上相当昂贵。就像在这些 GPU 机器上运行这些东西是相当昂贵的。因此，通常这些公司从第一天起就需要有一个盈利模式。我真的很高兴地说，这些上的大部分人工智能都在 Stripe 上运行，我们正在努力确保满足他们的所有需求。 (01:02:51)：例如，开放人工智能，利用我们通过聊天 GPT plus 和他们所有其他产品获利。但他们并不止于此。我们实际上正在帮助他们支持所有订阅、收入跟踪以及围绕业务的财务运营。重点是，我们多年来一直在这方面投入非常大的工程团队，这意味着任何想要构建对账产品和订阅业务模型的人，如果你想自己做，你就必须投入大型工程团队。但如果您可以使用 Stripe，您实际上可以将那些真正宝贵的工程资源集中在跟上该领域的惊人创新速度。所以我们对此感到很兴奋，但我们也对这些人工智能技术在我们自己更好地服务用户的能力上的应用感到非常兴奋。例如，在会议上我们将讨论其中的一些内容。 (01:03:44)：当 OpenAI 推出测试版时，我们就开始与他们合作。这是今年年初推出的 GPT 4 的一种私人测试版。我们首先想到的是我们有很多关于 Stripe 的文档，并且我们投入了大量的精力来使其变得更好。但是，如果您想通过 Stripe 集成实现某些目标，您通常会花费大量时间阅读文档并以最终用户的身份综合它们。我们意识到我们可以让 GPT 4 读取我们的所有文档，将它们存储为嵌入，然后回答开发人员的问题。因此，我们现在在文档中提供了早期版本。事实证明它非常有价值。我们还能够将这些技术应用到我们产品的其他领域。因此，我们将在 IT 会议的早期版本中展示的是，我们有一个非常强大的产品，作为我们的收入和财务自动化套件的一部分，我们称之为 Sigma。 (01:04:36)：它允许您在所有 Stripe 数据中编写后续查询，以便您可以查询 Stripe 数据以了解您的业务和真正细粒度的细节。哪个国家的销售额增长最快，哪个国家的哪个细分市场具有特殊属性？非常强大的产品，但对于非开发人员来说采用它可能具有挑战性。您确实必须知道如何编写后续查询，除非您只是使用菜单中的查询来充分发挥产品的价值。事实证明，对于大型语言模型，我们可以应用这项技术，您可以用自然语言提出问题，我们的引擎实际上会为您编写后续查询。我们必须做很多工作来调整它，以确保它可靠、易于理解，并且进展顺利。我们还看到了这些技术在实际应用中的出色应用，使我们的内部效率更高，更快地回答用户问题，更快地互相帮助。所以我们也在做这些事情。我们所做的一件具体的事情，令我非常兴奋的是，在我们看到聊天 GPT 出现后不久，我们意识到如果我们能够将其应用到 Stripe 内的许多用例中，那将是非常棒的。但正如你可以想象的那样，我们每天处理的很多数据对我们的业务、我们的用户非常敏感，我们非常关心，我们对此有很多治理，但我们希望制定这项技术法案。我们不能说，嘿 Stripes，去使用聊天 GPT。因此，我们建立了与 GPT 4 的集成和内部 UI 来使用此类模型。但这是我想与所有观众产生共鸣的事情。我们发现我们在其中内置了预设。 (01:06:12)：因此，当您使用大型语言模型时，您需要编写一个提示，帮助模型进入能够解决当前特定问题的状态。我们发现，许多不同工作类别的人们都可以编写提示，而不仅仅是工程师。我们营销团队的人员、用户支持团队的人员也已经能够使用它。但是，您可以花很多心思和精力来获得真正有效的提示，但我们无法让这些提示在整个公司内共享。因此，我可以获取预设来帮助我以正确的语气撰写博客文章，我发现它对于帮助我和公司的许多其他人非常有价值。因此，我认为高端公司有很多创新服务于他们的用户，并且现在就可以运营，我们正在努力代表我们的用户利用所有这些创新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about as engineers? Are pro co-pilot, is there some along those lines that you find useful weary of? How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 作为工程师呢？作为专业副驾驶，您是否觉得有些有用的厌倦？您对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: We're excited about co-pilot. We've made co-pilot available to our engineers internally. We ran a fairly rigorous trial to make sure that we felt good about its actual impact on our ability to write code and the code it was actually generating and find that it was very effective for us. Both in productivity but also just in helping our engineers feel like they could direct their energy towards some of the bigger problems. How should this stuff fit together rather than some of the micro problems. So because we had such great feedback on that, we've made it available very broadly internally and we'll be very excited to see where that space develops over time.
turns.zh: 我们对副驾驶感到很兴奋。我们已经在内部为我们的工程师提供了副驾驶。我们进行了相当严格的试验，以确保我们对它对我们编写代码的能力以及它实际生成的代码的实际影响感到满意，并发现它对我们非常有效。无论是在生产力方面，还是在帮助我们的工程师感觉他们可以将精力集中到一些更大的问题上。这些东西应该如何组合在一起而不是一些微观问题。因此，因为我们对此得到了非常好的反馈，所以我们在内部非常广泛地提供了它，我们将非常高兴地看到这个空间随着时间的推移而发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a sense of the productivity gain that say imagine you have a lot of 10X engineers, the gains that an amazing engineer gets out of a co-pilot versus a newer engineer?
turns.zh: 假设您有很多 10X 工程师，您是否对生产力的提高有感觉，即一位出色的工程师从副驾驶那里获得的收益与新工程师相比？

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: It's honestly too early to tell because we've only recently made it available at scale. What we're typically seeing is that the kind of tasks that it accelerates are, remember I mentioned how much energy we put into having comprehensive test suites. It's actually using co-pilot to generate your test cases, turns out to be extremely valuable. There's a reasonable amount of boiler plate that is kind of like repeated code and concepts that goes into writing good tests. But you also have to reason very carefully about is this actually testing is exactly what I want? So co-pilot takes a lot of that boiler plate generation out of the way. So you're actually thinking about the stuff that really matters. And I think that is going to have a profound impact on quality of code that we write as well. But it's a little too early to say, because we literally just folded out what kind of actual measurable impact is having.
turns.zh: 老实说，现在下结论还为时过早，因为我们最近才大规模提供它。我们通常看到的是，它加速的任务类型是，记住我提到过我们在全面的测试套件上投入了多少精力。它实际上是使用副驾驶来生成测试用例，事实证明这是非常有价值的。有相当数量的样板，有点像编写好的测试所需的重复代码和概念。但你也必须非常仔细地思考这是否真的是我想要的测试？因此，副驾驶消除了很多样板生成过程。所以你实际上正在考虑真正重要的事情。我认为这也会对我们编写的代码质量产生深远的影响。但现在说还为时过早，因为我们实际上只是列出了正在产生的实际可衡量的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was talking to an engineer and he's just like, I like the active writing code and it makes me sad that this is doing this for me. So he turns it off.
turns.zh: 我正在和一位工程师交谈，他就像，我喜欢积极地编写代码，这让我很难过，这是为我做的。所以他把它关掉了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is doing this for me, so he turns it off. I think over time people will be like, "Eh, that's true. I never really enjoyed this part of it."
turns.zh: 这是为我做的，所以他把它关掉了。我想随着时间的推移，人们会说，“呃，那是真的。我从来没有真正喜欢过这一部分。”

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: Yeah, I'll speak from personal experience. I love writing code. I really love writing code. It's pretty much what I do for fun. I also love writing code with Copilot, because as I said, it means that I can focus on the parts that really matter. I think that's been a fairly consistent experience across Stripe as well.
turns.zh: 是的，我就从个人经历来说说。我喜欢写代码。我真的很喜欢写代码。这几乎就是我为了好玩而做的事情。我也喜欢使用 Copilot 编写代码，因为正如我所说，这意味着我可以专注于真正重要的部分。我认为这在 Stripe 上也是相当一致的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You run a massive engineering team. I don't know if you shared the numbers of engineers, but I know there are many. What are, and this is a broad question, just what are some lessons you've learned about managing people and/or managing engineers, whichever direction you want to go?
turns.zh: 惊人的。您管理着一支庞大的工程团队。我不知道你是否分享了工程师的数量，但我知道有很多。这是一个广泛的问题，您在管理人员和/或管理工程师方面学到了哪些经验教训，无论您想朝哪个方向发展？

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: Wow, big question. There are so many different directions we could take that. I'll share a few observations. They don't necessarily all have a particular theme to them. I think as I've been responsible for bigger and bigger teams over time, one of the things that just I repeatedly learn is I personally will not be involved in really any of the decisions that matter and happen. There are thousands of decisions that an organization of any skill is making every single day, every individual engineer or PM is making hundreds of small decisions and some big ones every day that affect the kind of general trajectory. (01:10:17): The most important thing is to really focus on hiring the right people, and that means hiring people that you can trust with a tremendous amount of autonomy. If I try to get involved in lots of decisions, everything will grind to a halt. How do you do that? It is important, obviously, to be rigorous. We've described already what our hiring process is. I really lean into getting to know folks in very, very well as we're hiring them. By the way, something I didn't mention earlier that is I think important here is we pay a lot of attention at Stripe during the hiring process to references. (01:10:49): This is typically later in the process, but if you put someone through an interview process, you've probably spent what, eight hours total with them? If you talk to people that actually have worked with them before, you're probably benefiting from thousands of hours of direct experience. We take this very seriously, and we try to ask smart questions that will help get real signal out of that. I certainly find when it comes to hiring folks that have then gone on to really make a transformative impact, that references are often the time that you get the best conviction on the hire or not. (01:11:22): Hire the right people, and then you have to trust them. Now, trust is interesting. Is actually quite challenging to trust people that you've just hired, right? Well, you've got no stake really on you yet. What I find is you do actually just have to be generous in giving trust and assuming trust by default at the beginning. Then you do need to hold people accountable enough that they are proving that they can handle that trust. Sometimes, that means hiring someone who you think quite plausibly can end up in a very big role into a smaller role to begin with. Other times, you just have the big role that you need to fill, in which case, it's important to be quite conscious about really trusting and delegating to them with a lot of support. (01:12:02): I'm always working hard to delegate sometimes a little bit more than I'm comfortable with, because that's the only way to really operate at significant scale. I think something else, and sorry, this is really a smorgasboard is what a lot of differences.
turns.zh: 哇，大问题。我们可以采取很多不同的方向。我将分享一些观察结果。它们不一定都有特定的主题。我认为，随着时间的推移，我一直负责越来越大的团队，我反复学到的一件事是，我个人不会真正参与任何重要和发生的决策。任何技能的组织每天都会做出数千个决策，每个工程师或 PM 每天都会做出数百个小决策和一些大决策，这些决策会影响总体轨迹。 (01:10:17)：最重要的是真正专注于雇用合适的人，这意味着雇用您可以信任且拥有巨大自主权的人。如果我试图参与很多决定，一切都会陷入停滞。你是怎么做到的？显然，严谨很重要。我们已经描述了我们的招聘流程。当我们雇用他们时，我真的很想非常非常了解他们。顺便说一句，我之前没有提到但我认为这里很重要的一点是，我们在 Stripe 在招聘过程中非常注重推荐人。 (01:10:49)：这通常是在流程的后期，但如果你让某人经历面试过程，你可能总共花了八个小时与他们在一起？如果您与以前实际共事过的人交谈，您可能会从数千小时的直接经验中受益。我们非常重视这一点，并尝试提出明智的问题，这将有助于从中获得真正的信号。我当然发现，当涉及到聘用那些真正产生变革性影响的人时，推荐信通常是你对聘用或不聘用最有信心的时候。 (01:11:22)：雇用合适的人，然后你必须信任他们。现在，信任很有趣。信任你刚刚雇佣的人实际上是很有挑战性的，对吧？好吧，你还没有真正的赌注。我发现你实际上只需要在开始时慷慨地给予信任并默认接受信任。那么你确实需要让人们承担足够的责任，以证明他们能够承受这种信任。有时，这意味着雇用一个你认为很有可能最终会担任一个非常大角色的人，然后开始扮演一个较小的角色。其他时候，你只是需要扮演重要的角色，在这种情况下，重要的是要非常有意识地真正信任他们并在大量支持下委派给他们。 (01:12:02)：我总是努力授权，有时会超出我的承受范围，因为这是真正大规模运营的唯一方法。我认为还有其他事情，抱歉，这确实是一个大杂烩，有很多差异。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美的。

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: Something else I've realized as the organizations I work with and been responsible for have grown is that you have to be extremely conscious about managing your own time. There are hundreds or thousands of people who, quite legitimately, might want to get some time with you. If you just let the places that you spend your time and energy be controlled by the stuff that comes into your inbox, or the stuff that gets put on your calendar, that's going to be random. It's quite likely that that's not laddering up to the biggest impact. I personally have been running a loop for, I don't know, maybe 10 years, where on Sunday evenings, and usually, well, it usually starts on Sunday afternoons, I read a lot of what happened last week. (01:12:59): Then on Sunday evenings, I actually write a list for myself of, you asked me a question at this podcast, which is like, what would be great success for this podcast from your perspective? (01:13:08): I basically think about that for my week every Sunday night. I make a list of if we got these things done this week, that is a good week, but obviously, we need to be dynamic. Things will surprise you through the week. Honestly, then, that drives a lot of just where I decide to spend my time. I try to encourage everyone to think that way throughout the organization. I think it does ladder up to more impact over time. I think the final thing I'll say here is I mentioned how important operating principles are to the culture. I think for any manager and any leaders, that includes ICPMs as well, but for any manager, any leader, how you show up really does set the culture that is around you. (01:13:50): I try very hard to show up very consistently every day, even though there will very frequently be things that are going wrong and are bad and are hard. It's actually very important to show up quite consistently. Certainly, in line with all the values that we have and the culture that we want to set, in order to really kind of model that at scale. Different days, that can be easier and harder. The final thing is, I think it's quite important to manage your own energy. (01:14:17): There are some tasks that I do that are maybe not the most important thing, but I know that I get a lot of joy and energy from them, and then that carries over into the other stuff that also needs to get done.
turns.zh: 随着我所工作和负责的组织的发展，我还意识到，你必须非常有意识地管理自己的时间。有成百上千的人可能想和你共度时光，这也是合理的。如果您只是让收件箱中的内容或日历上的内容来控制您花费时间和精力的地方，那么这将是随机的。这很可能还没有达到最大的影响。我个人已经循环运行了，我不知道，也许有10年了，在周日晚上，通常，嗯，通常从周日下午开始，我读了很多上周发生的事情。 (01:12:59)：然后在周日晚上，我实际上为自己写了一个清单，你在这个播客中问了我一个问题，就像，从你的角度来看，这个播客的巨大成功是什么？ (01:13:08)：我基本上每周日晚上都会考虑这一周。我列出了一个清单，如果我们本周完成了这些事情，那将是美好的一周，但显然，我们需要充满活力。这周的事情会让你感到惊讶。老实说，这在很大程度上决定了我决定把时间花在哪里。我试图鼓励整个组织中的每个人都这样思考。我认为随着时间的推移，它确实会产生更大的影响。我想我要说的最后一件事是我提到了运营原则对文化的重要性。我认为对于任何经理和任何领导者来说，这也包括 ICPM，但对于任何经理、任何领导者来说，你的表现确实会影响你周围的文化。 (01:13:50)：我每天都非常努力地表现得始终如一，尽管经常会出现一些问题、不好的事情和困难的事情。事实上，保持一致的表现非常重要。当然，这符合我们拥有的所有价值观和我们想要设定的文化，以便真正大规模地建立模型。不同的日子，可能会更容易，也可能更困难。最后一点是，我认为管理好自己的精力是非常重要的。 (01:14:17)：我所做的一些任务可能不是最重要的事情，但我知道我从中获得了很多快乐和能量，然后这会延续到其他也需要完成的事情中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just two more questions before we get to our very exciting lightning round. One is just I feel like Stripe is incredibly good at planning and organizing, prioritizing. I know every inside, it's always not as beautiful as it may seem on the outside, but what have you learned? What has Stripe learned about planning and prioritizing that you think other companies might be missing?
turns.zh: 在我们进入非常激动人心的闪电回合之前，还有两个问题。一是我觉得 Stripe 非常擅长规划、组织和确定优先级。我知道每一个里面，它总是不像外表看起来那么美丽，但是你学到了什么？ Stripe 在规划和优先级方面学到了哪些您认为其他公司可能缺少的知识？

turns.speaker: David Singleton
turns.en: Yeah. Well it's funny you say that. I would say planning inside of Stripe does not get the highest net promoter score that you might imagine. I do think it is actually quite effective. By the way, the reason I think that planning, the way we do planning at Stripe doesn't always get the best internal rep is we have grown very rapidly. That means that almost every time we come back around to planning, we actually, and this is kind of a theme at Stripe, we think about a lot of the ways that we work internally from First principles. (01:15:19): We will tend not to by default just pick a system off of the shelf that some other company has run or that we've used before. We'll think hard, considering what we are doing for our users. How should we do this? When we're thinking even first principles, we'll often go out and talk to a lot of other companies, and try to learn from their experience. It's actually something I've really appreciated and enjoyed at Stripe. A lot of the learning I've done here has come not only from folks that are at the company, but also talking to a bunch of folks that we have the privilege to work closely with because their business is building on Stripe, or they're a similar stage of scale to us. (01:15:56): A good example of this is Amazon. Amazon is a Stripe user. Because we work with them, in my first couple of weeks at Stripe, I was actually able to meet with Charlie Bell, who then ran operations at Stripe. A lot of the things that, sorry, who then ran operations at Amazon. A lot of the things that we actually now do at Stripe have come from learning from that experience. It wasn't just, oh yeah, we'll take this thing cause Amazon did it, talk to him. Lots of other companies hard to learn. The point is we care about learning from others and then we apply it. (01:16:21): Bringing this back to planning, because we tend to think a lot from first principles and we've been growing rapidly. The right planning process for us as a company has actually changed quite dramatically and quite significantly over the years. We do planning in a relatively deep way once a year, and then in a slightly lighter way halfway through the year. If you imagine doing someone once a year and you're growing rapidly, you're going to want to revisit exactly how you do it. I think for anyone who has the privilege of running the same planning process again and again, you can really iterate it and tune it. We've had to make more deliberate and more sweeping changes as we've gone along. There are a couple things at the core of how we do this. One is it's really important to focus on who are the users that we are seeking to serve for any given product area that we're working in? Kind of holding their needs front and center in your plans is important. Again, at Stripe, we do something that is, it's not unconventional, but it's not the most common practice in the industry, which is we work very hard to serve companies from the very, very small. The folks that are literally just starting their company on Stripe, with Stripe Atlas, all the way up to multinational, 10 Fortune five companies, fortune one companies, I guess. (01:17:39): There's a very different set of user needs across those businesses. For any given area, it's very important for each team to be clear about who are they serving. Then we run a kind of inverted W process. We typically have teams surface what their immediate thoughts are on the most important things to do. We'll then have a group of product leaders get together and try to synthesize the most important parts of that into a kind of draft overall company strategy, and then take that back down to teams to figure out, "Well, if that's where we're making a big push, should that tweak my plans at all?" (01:18:13): We bring it back up for synthesis, and then back down for everyone to really distribute with a lot of context within their orgs. We find that at our current scale, very, very effective.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，你这么说很有趣。我想说的是，在 Stripe 内部进行规划并不会获得您想象中的最高净推荐值。我确实认为这实际上非常有效。顺便说一句，我认为我们在 Stripe 进行规划的方式并不总能获得最好的内部代表的原因是我们发展得非常快。这意味着几乎每次我们回到规划时，实际上，这也是 Stripe 的一个主题，我们会根据第一原则思考我们内部工作的很多方式。 (01:15:19)：默认情况下，我们不会倾向于直接选择其他公司已经运行或我们以前使用过的现成系统。我们会认真思考，考虑我们为用户所做的事情。我们应该怎样做呢？当我们思考首要原则时，我们经常会出去与许多其他公司交谈，并尝试从他们的经验中学习。这实际上是我在 Stripe 非常欣赏和享受的事情。我在这里学到的很多东西不仅来自公司内部的人员，还来自与我们有幸密切合作的一群人的交谈，因为他们的业务是建立在 Stripe 上的，或者他们的规模与我们相似。 (01:15:56)：亚马逊就是一个很好的例子。亚马逊是 Stripe 用户。因为我们与他们合作，在我加入 Stripe 的头几周，我实际上能够见到 Charlie Bell，他后来负责 Stripe 的运营。抱歉，很多事情都是后来在亚马逊运营的。我们现在在 Stripe 所做的很多事情都是从那次经历中学习的。这不仅仅是，哦，是的，我们会接受这件事，因为亚马逊做到了，与他交谈。很多其他公司很难学习。关键是我们关心向他人学习，然后应用它。 (01:16:21)：回到规划中来，因为我们倾向于从基本原则出发思考很多，而且我们一直在快速发展。多年来，我们作为一家公司的正确规划流程实际上已经发生了巨大的变化。我们每年做一次比较深入的规划，然后到了中间再做一个稍微轻松一点的规划。如果你想象每年为某人做一次并且你正在快速成长，你就会想重新审视你是如何做的。我认为，对于任何有幸一次又一次运行相同规划流程的人来说，您都可以真正对其进行迭代和调整。随着我们的发展，我们必须做出更深思熟虑、更彻底的改变。我们如何做到这一点的核心有几件事。一是关注我们正在工作的任何给定产品领域寻求服务的用户是谁真的很重要？在你的计划中将他们的需求放在首位很重要。同样，在 Stripe，我们所做的事情并不是非常规的，但也不是行业中最常见的做法，即我们非常努力地为非常非常小的公司提供服务。我猜，这些人实际上刚刚在 Stripe 上创办自己的公司，通过 Stripe Atlas，一直到跨国公司、10 家《财富》五强公司、《财富》第一家公司。 (01:17:39)：这些企业的用户需求非常不同。对于任何特定区域，每个团队都必须清楚他们为谁服务，这一点非常重要。然后我们运行一种倒置的 W 过程。我们通常会让团队表达他们对最重要的事情的直接想法。然后，我们将让一组产品负责人聚在一起，尝试将其中最重要的部分综合成一种公司整体战略草案，然后将其带回给团队来弄清楚，“好吧，如果这是我们大力推动的领域，是否应该调整我的计划？” (01:18:13)：我们将其重新进行综合，然后将其重新放回，以便每个人在其组织内根据大量上下文进行真正的分发。我们发现，以我们目前的规模来看，这非常非常有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny

If I may actually just take one second, it's a really good example of how focusing on the needs of our users in one area took us into a really valuable space to solve for many users in other areas. (01:20:55): The ideas behind Stripe Connect came from working with companies like Lyft and Shopify. In the very early days, they were using Stripe for pay-ins, but we realized, "Oh, these companies are operating these multi-sided marketplaces, and there's a ton of heavy lifting you have to do to make that work really well." We have to have a bunch of regulatory licenses in place, but also there's a lot that you need to do to actually make the money move and kind of account for it in the right way. Connect is our product for platforms and marketplaces. (01:21:18): One of the things that we've done over the course of the last year or so is actually taken a lot of the features that we've built in the Stripe Dashboard to help folks manage things like gathering the right documents from their users, or handling refunds and so forth. We've actually made them available as embed-able UI components that are also completely customizable, which these platforms can take and put inside their own dashboards so they can present a lot of the power that Stripe is enabling to their customers, without having to do a ton of engineering work themselves. (01:21:53): Look, generating engineering leverage for our customers is just very frequently the main thing that we can do to help their businesses. We're going to show a bunch of that stuff next week, which I'm excited about. Then finally, we touched on it already, but it'll be great to show some of the innovation we've had around AI and large language models. Again, I think it's going to make a big impact over the coming years.
turns.zh: 我们已经在本次电话会议上讨论了我们在 Stripe Sessions 上首次广泛分享的一些内容。根据我们的开发流程，这些已经在一些 Stripe 用户手中掌握了相当长的时间，我们确实是与他们一起制作了它们。我对我们下周要讨论的一些事情感到非常兴奋。一是我提到了我们的收入和财务自动化套件。 (01:19:48)：我们确实已经在那里制作功能有一段时间了，这确实是一个很好的例子，说明与用户密切合作如何真正帮助大规模构建东西。我们与 Atlassian 和 CloudFlare 等公司合作提供了一系列功能，使他们的业务能够在 Stripe Billing 上运行。他们有相对复杂的模型。例如，您可能会签署一项协议，其中第一年有折扣，然后第二年使用另一种产品，然后第三年发生其他情况。您现在可以在 Stripe Billing 中对所有这些进行建模，我们将在下周的 Stripe Sessions 的仪表板中展示如何做到这一点。 (01:20:23)：现在所有 Stripe 用户都可以使用它。它为我们所有的用户（无论规模大小）提供了与世界上最好的 SAS 平台相同的能力。对此感到兴奋。我们在这次电话会议中也没有讨论这一点，Stripe Connect 是我们针对市场平台的产品。如果我真的可以花一秒钟时间，这是一个很好的例子，说明了关注某一领域用户的需求如何使我们进入一个非常有价值的空间，为其他领域的许多用户提供解决方案。 (01:20:55)：Stripe Connect 背后的想法来自于与 Lyft 和 Shopify 等公司的合作。在很早的时候，他们使用 Stripe 进行支付，但我们意识到，“哦，这些公司正在运营这些多边市场，你必须做大量的繁重工作才能使其真正发挥作用。”我们必须拥有一系列监管许可证，但还需要做很多事情才能真正使资金流动并以正确的方式对其进行核算。 Connect 是我们针对平台和市场的产品。 (01:21:18)：我们在过去一年左右所做的事情之一实际上是采用了我们在 Stripe 仪表板中构建的许多功能来帮助人们管理诸如从用户那里收集正确的文档或处理退款等事务。实际上，我们已经将它们作为可嵌入的 UI 组件提供，这些组件也是完全可定制的，这些平台可以将其放入自己的仪表板中，这样它们就可以向客户展示 Stripe 所提供的大量功能，而无需自己做大量的工程工作。 (01:21:53)：看，为我们的客户创造工程影响力通常是我们可以帮助他们的业务做的主要事情。下周我们将展示很多这样的东西，我对此感到很兴奋。最后，我们已经谈到了它，但如果能展示我们在人工智能和大型语言模型方面的一些创新，那就太好了。我再次认为这将在未来几年产生重大影响。

turns.zh: 好吧，实际上，你会在本书中找到我推荐的一些面试问题。事实上，我真的很喜欢一个问题，因为这听起来像垒球，但事实并非如此，我经常问人们，尤其是领导力招聘方面，他们最钦佩与哪位领导者共事以及为什么。这听起来像是一个垒球，但它实际上告诉你很多关于这个人在领导力方面真正关心的是什么。 (01:24:55)：有时，我会跟进并问：“这在您自己的领导风格中有何体现？”然后，我认为这确实很有说服力，我总是问人们，我会破坏我的面试问题，我会在你的播客中透露它，但我总是问人们，“好吧，假设你是他们的经理。告诉我你会给他们提供的绩效评估或发展反馈，以帮助他们提高效率。”我认为每个人总有可以改进的地方，当然包括我自己。 (01:25:22)：我觉得人们能够批判性地思考他们所钦佩或崇拜的人，以及他们如何才能真正变得更有效，这很能说明问题。
